explanation: Phenylketonuria is correctly matched with phenylpyruvate; the disease causes phenylalanine accumulation and its transamination products (phenylpyruvate, phenylacetate, phenyllactate) are excreted.
In PKU, phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency leads to inability to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine, resulting in tyrosine deficiency and catecholamine synthesis impairment.
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome in chronic alcoholics presents with the classic triad of confusion, ataxia, and memory impairment due to thiamine (B1) deficiency.
Thiamine pyrophosphate is a cofactor for alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; its deficiency impairs this enzyme causing neurological dysfunction in Wernicke-Korsakoff.
Folic acid (as N5, N10-methylenetetrahydrofolate) provides one-carbon units for thymidylate synthase and purine synthesis reactions in nucleotide biosynthesis.
Thiamine (vitamin B1) is essential for oxidative decarboxylation reactions catalyzed by pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
The triad of diarrhea, dementia, and dermatitis (photosensitive rash) is classic for pellagra caused by niacin (vitamin B3) deficiency.
Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration of the cord; folic acid can mask the anemia but does not prevent neurological progression.
Sulfonamides competitively inhibit dihydropteroate synthase, blocking folic acid synthesis in bacteria (humans obtain folate from diet, not synthesis).
Homocysteine remethylation to methionine requires methyltetrahydrofolate (from folic acid) as methyl donor and methionine synthase (which needs B12).
Methyltetrahydrofolate donates its methyl group to homocysteine via methionine synthase (requiring B12) to regenerate methionine.
Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is the essential cofactor for aromatic amino acid hydroxylases including phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan hydroxylases.
Homocysteine to methionine conversion requires both vitamin B12 (as methylcobalamin) and folic acid (as methyltetrahydrofolate) for the methionine synthase reaction.
Astrocytes perform gliosis (reactive astrogliosis) in response to CNS injury, forming glial scars; they also maintain the blood-brain barrier and ion balance.
The outer band of Baillarger (optic radiation fibers) is found in the inner granular layer (layer IV) of the cerebral cortex, while the inner band is in layer V.
In Pacinian corpuscles, the afferent fiber passes axially through the center, while in Meissner corpuscles the nerve fiber has a coiled (tortuous) course between lamellar cells.
Proprioception receptors (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, joint receptors) provide information about body position, movement, and limb location in space.
The nerve fiber in Meissner's corpuscle has a characteristic tortuous (coiled) course between the lamellar cells, unlike the straight axial course in Pacinian corpuscles.
Meissner's corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors in the dermal papillae that detect crude touch and tactile discrimination, particularly in glabrous skin.
Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting deep pressure and vibration receptors with a characteristic onion-like lamellar structure located in dermis and deeper tissues.
Both free nerve endings and Merkel's discs are found in the epidermis; free nerve endings detect pain and temperature while Merkel discs detect light touch.
The cornea contains abundant free nerve endings (no specific encapsulated receptors) making it extremely sensitive to pain and touch.
Free nerve endings and Merkel discs both penetrate the epidermis; free nerve endings respond to pain/temperature while Merkel discs mediate light touch.
Substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) is located in lamina II of the spinal cord gray matter and processes pain and temperature sensations.
Clarke's nucleus (dorsocentral nucleus) is present at all thoracic levels (T1-L2) and is the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
Clarke's nucleus is found in lamina VII (intermediate gray matter) at cervical levels, serving as the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
The posteromarginal nucleus is located in lamina I of the spinal cord and receives pain and temperature afferents from the periphery.
Gamma motor neurons innervate intrafusal muscle fibers within muscle spindles, regulating spindle sensitivity and the stretch reflex loop.
The anteromedial nucleus (in the anterior horn) has motor function, containing motor neuron pools for axial and proximal limb muscles.
Methadone is a long-acting pure mu-opioid agonist used in opioid maintenance therapy, producing milder withdrawal due to its slow dissociation from receptors.
Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist that rapidly reverses heroin intoxication by blocking mu-opioid receptors, restoring respiratory drive.
Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist and kappa antagonist, producing ceiling effects on respiratory depression and milder withdrawal.
Naltrexone is a long-acting opioid antagonist used to prevent relapse in alcohol dependence by blocking opioid receptors involved in reward pathways.
Naloxone, like naltrexone, is an opioid antagonist that can reverse fentanyl intoxication by competitively blocking opioid receptors.
Tramadol is a mixed mechanism analgesic with both mu-opioid agonist activity and inhibition of serotonin/norepinephrine reuptake, unlike pure morphine.
